title: 04 — Time Series Forecasting and Nowcasting
html:
04 — Time Series Forecasting and Nowcasting

The one idea: a forecast is only as good as the simplest baseline it beats, measured the way it will be used: train on the past, predict the next period, step forward, repeat. Seasonality and calendar effects usually matter more than the choice of algorithm.

1. What it is

  • Time series: values measured over time, such as monthly industry inflows, daily NAVs or quarterly credit growth.
  • Forecasting: predicting future values.
  • Nowcasting: estimating the current or just-finished period before official data arrives, from faster indicators. For example, this month's credit growth from weekly data.
  • Components:
    • trend (long-run direction),
    • seasonality (repeating calendar patterns, such as quarter-end or financial-year-end),
    • events (policy changes, crises),
    • noise.

2. Why it matters

  • Nowcasts, sector-stress estimates and flow forecasts are intelligence products. Each needs a published method and an honest track record.
  • Time-ordered data breaks random splits: a model that sees next month during training looks brilliant and fails live.
  • Bitemporal storage lets you rebuild exactly what was known at each past forecast date, which an honest backtest needs.

3. The main ideas, beginner to expert

3.1 Beginner: always start with baselines

Baseline Forecast Beats it when
Naive Last value There is a trend or seasonality
Seasonal naive Value from the same period last year Seasonality dominates
Moving average Mean of the last k periods Noise dominates

If a sophisticated model can't beat seasonal naive, don't ship it.

3.2 Intermediate: walk-forward backtesting

---
title: Walk-forward backtest — the model never sees the future
---
flowchart LR
    A["Train: months 1..48"] --> P1["Predict 49"]
    B["Train: months 1..49"] --> P2["Predict 50"]
    C["Train: months 1..50"] --> P3["Predict 51"]
    P1 --> E["Collect errors,<br/>compare methods"]
    P2 --> E
    P3 --> E

Metrics:

  • MAE: mean absolute error, in the units of the data.
  • MAPE: percentage error. Unstable near zero, so avoid it for flows that cross zero.
  • MASE: MAE divided by the in-sample naive MAE. Below 1 means better than naive, and it is comparable across series.

Also report errors on the periods that matter (quarter-ends, March).

3.3 Senior: models and nowcasts

Approach Use
Linear models with lags, trend and calendar dummies Strong, explainable default
ETS (exponential smoothing), ARIMA and SARIMA (statsmodels) Classical single-series forecasting
Gradient boosting on lag and calendar features (03) Many related series, with external drivers
Mixed-frequency regression Nowcasting a monthly or quarterly figure from weekly or daily indicators
Deep and foundation time-series models Large panels. Validate carefully against baselines

Nowcasting rules:

  • Use only indicators published before the nowcast time. Store their vintages, since early releases get revised.
  • Record each nowcast with its input vintage, method version and the realised value when it arrives. That record is the published track record.

4. Working code

The script makes six years of made-up monthly inflows with a trend and a March dip, then backtests four methods walk-forward over the last 24 months. numpy only.

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
# Made-up monthly industry net inflows (crore) with trend, a March-quarter-end dip, and noise.
months = 72
t = np.arange(months)
season = np.where(t % 12 == 2, -900.0, 0.0) + np.where(t % 12 == 3, 400.0, 0.0)   # March dip, April rebound
y = 2000 + 25 * t + season + rng.normal(0, 250, months)

# Forecasting methods, each using ONLY data before the month it predicts.
def naive(hist):          return hist[-1]
def seasonal_naive(hist): return hist[-12]
def mean_3(hist):         return hist[-3:].mean()
def ar_with_season(hist):
    # Linear model: y_t ~ a + b*t + c*y_{t-1} + d*[March] + e*[April], fitted by least squares on history.
    n = len(hist)
    rows = [[1, i, hist[i - 1], i % 12 == 2, i % 12 == 3] for i in range(1, n)]
    coef, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(np.array(rows, float), hist[1:], rcond=None)
    return float(np.array([1, n, hist[-1], n % 12 == 2, n % 12 == 3], float) @ coef)

# Walk-forward backtest: for each of the last 24 months, train on everything before it, predict it.
methods = {"naive": naive, "seasonal naive": seasonal_naive, "3-month mean": mean_3, "trend+AR+season": ar_with_season}
errors = {m: [] for m in methods}
for cut in range(months - 24, months):
    for name, f in methods.items():
        errors[name].append(y[cut] - f(y[:cut]))
scale = np.mean(np.abs(np.diff(y[:months - 24])))          # MASE scale: in-sample naive error
for name, e in errors.items():
    e = np.array(e)
    print(f"{name:16s} MAE {np.mean(np.abs(e)):6.1f}  MASE {np.mean(np.abs(e)) / scale:.2f}  "
          f"March MAE {np.mean(np.abs(e[[i for i in range(24) if (months - 24 + i) % 12 == 2]])):6.1f}")

# The leakage trap: a random train/test split lets the model see the future around each test month.
print("Random-split evaluation would mix future months into training; walk-forward never does.")

Output:

naive            MAE  409.1  MASE 1.01  March MAE  762.0
seasonal naive   MAE  366.6  MASE 0.90  March MAE  427.2
3-month mean     MAE  289.6  MASE 0.71  March MAE  764.7
trend+AR+season  MAE  199.4  MASE 0.49  March MAE  308.5
Random-split evaluation would mix future months into training; walk-forward never does.

What to notice:

  • Seasonal naive beats naive (MASE 0.90 vs 1.01), because the March dip repeats.
  • The 3-month mean has a good overall MAE but the worst March error (764.7). Averages hide failures in exactly the periods people care about.
  • The linear model with trend, a lag and March and April dummies halves the naive error (MASE 0.49) and handles March best. Calendar knowledge beats a cleverer algorithm.

5. Common mistakes

  1. Random train and test splits on time series.
  2. Using revised data to backtest a nowcast. Use the vintage available on each date.
  3. No baseline. A complex model must beat seasonal naive.
  4. MAPE on series near zero. Use MAE or MASE.
  5. Ignoring calendar effects: quarter-ends, financial-year-end, holidays, and the number of business days.

6. Exercise (1.5 hours)

  1. Add a 12-month moving-average method and an exponential smoothing method (level = a*y + (1-a)*level), and backtest them.
  2. Change the March dip to start only from year 4 (a policy change), and see which methods adapt.
  3. Turn the linear model into a nowcast: predict this month using a made-up weekly indicator available halfway through the month.

7. Questions to test yourself

  1. Why must time-series evaluation be walk-forward?
  2. What does a MASE below 1 mean?
  3. Why can an average error hide a serious problem?
  4. What makes a nowcast's backtest honest?
  5. Why record each nowcast with its input vintage?

Answers

  1. Each prediction must use only data from before it, as in real use. Random splits leak the future.
  2. The method's mean absolute error is lower than the in-sample naive forecast's.
  3. Large errors in key periods (such as March) are diluted by many easy periods.
  4. Using only data and indicator vintages available at each past nowcast time.
  5. So the forecast can be reproduced and the track record audited later.

8. Sources

Checked 2026-10-26.
